subtitle: Practice planning for several plausible futures instead of one forecast. You will scan for change, build simple scenarios with the people affected, test decisions for who is most exposed and plan what you leave in place.
audience: For senior leaders, managers of managers and program leads who plan beyond the next budget cycle and want their plans to hold up when conditions change. Anyone who shapes long-term work will also find it useful.

lessons.title: Why foresight matters in public service
objectives: Explain the difference between relying on a single forecast and preparing for several plausible futures.
Distinguish expected, alternative and preferred futures in a plan you know.
Identify one assumption in a current plan that treats the future as an extension of the present.
Describe how your own vantage point shapes which future seems most likely to you.
lessons.teaching:
A budget request, staffing plan or five-year goal may assume that current conditions will continue. Make that assumption visible rather than treating it as a fact. That works when conditions are steady. It works less well when the system itself changes, as it does when a workforce shrinks, a population ages or a funding stream ends. The Government Office for Science's Futures Toolkit draws the distinction this way: most forecasting models project past trends on a fixed view of how the system works, while futures thinking allows for change in the system itself. Forecasts can also present ranges and probabilities. Here, the comparison is with relying on a single forecast. Looking further ahead invites consideration of a wider range of plausible changes.

Foresight means preparing for several futures instead of betting on one. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's foresight guide separates three kinds: the expected future, what we think will happen; alternative futures, what might happen instead; and the preferred future, what we want to happen. Holding all three in view keeps a plan honest and helps a leader tell a prediction from a hope. OPM says foresight complements a federal agency's required strategic planning rather than replacing it. The U.S. Government Accountability Office's Center for Strategic Foresight publishes trend papers that look five to 15 years ahead, a useful reminder that your own plan can look beyond one budget cycle.

Which future looks likely depends on where you stand. A leader's sense of the normal course of events is learned, and it is shaped by the people, data and communities that leader sees most often. If planning data counts only people who already use a service, the expected future quietly leaves out people who could not reach it. If a planning team shares one background or one work location, it may share the same blind spots. OPM's guide names cognitive bias directly and lists awareness of underlying assumptions among the benefits of foresight. Asking whose future a plan describes is an equity question and a quality question at once.

Foresight can start with one plan you already know. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide lists strategic thinking and vision setting among the skills expected of leaders of an organization, and this is one practical way to build them. Write down the future your plan assumes. Ask what would have to be true for it to arrive, what might happen instead, and who would feel the difference first. Bring the question to people who see the work from another position. Foresight supports better questions; it does not change what a law, rule or contract requires, and decisions stay with the areas responsible for them.
lessons.keyPoint: A single forecast leaves assumptions to test. Compare expected, alternative and preferred futures, ask whose experience each reflects, and use evidence to revisit the plan.
lessons.example: Practice case: Marisol, a deputy director in disability services, is preparing a five-year plan for waiver services. Glenn, a senior analyst, has built a careful forecast of demand and direct support workforce capacity from the last eight years of data. Leadership wants one planning number by Friday. Marisol notices that the forecast assumes the direct support workforce keeps its current size and that people on waiting lists enroll at past rates. Neither assumption is certain. This is an initial planning estimate, not a final service or funding decision. No required study or consultation is being displaced by the Friday deadline.
lessons.question: What should Marisol do with the forecast?
choices: Submit Glenn's forecast as the planning number, since it is the best data the team has and leadership asked for a single figure this week.
Hold the plan until the team can commission a fuller workforce study, so the five-year numbers rest on stronger and more current evidence.
Submit the forecast as the expected future and add two short alternative futures that change the workforce and enrollment assumptions.
feedback: The forecast is useful, but presenting it alone hides two open assumptions. If the workforce shrinks, people waiting for services feel it first, and the plan has no answer ready.

Seek better evidence where it is needed, and identify decisions that must wait for it. For this initial estimate, alternatives can show uncertainty without holding up the whole submission. A deadline never replaces a required review.
This is the recommended step. It keeps Glenn's careful work, meets the deadline and shows leaders what the plan depends on, so they can watch the right signals and prepare.
lessons.reflection: Think of a plan you rely on at work. What future does it quietly assume, and where did you first learn to expect that future?
lessons.action: Pick one plan, budget or project you are part of. Write one sentence naming the future it assumes and two sentences describing a plausible alternative. Note who would feel the difference first.

check.question: Compared with relying on the single forecast in this case, what does foresight add?
check.correct: Foresight prepares for several plausible futures, while a forecast projects one.
wrong: Foresight uses better data, so its single prediction is more likely to be right.
Foresight describes the future we hope for, while a forecast relies on evidence.
check.feedback: The forecast in this case presents one expected future. Foresight adds plausible alternatives and a preferred future to test the plan. Forecasting can also use ranges and probabilities; the distinction here is from relying on just one projection.

lessons.title: Scanning, drivers and scenarios with the people affected
objectives: Plan a short horizon scanning and driver mapping exercise around one scoping question.
Build four plausible scenarios from two important uncertainties, then compare at least two of them.
Use examples of Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation to examine planning assumptions without assessing a person or team.
Design one change that lets people affected by a plan help imagine its futures.
lessons.teaching:
Horizon scanning, driver mapping and scenarios are three simple foresight tools. The Futures Toolkit groups its methods under three questions: what is changing, so what for our futures, and now what do we do. Each exercise starts with a scoping question that sets the topic and a time frame, often ten years or more. Horizon scanning gathers signs of change from many sources, including ones outside your usual field. OPM's foresight guide calls an early indicator of an issue that may matter later a weak signal. It offers scanning frameworks built on social, technological, economic, environmental and political factors, and advises including social factors in every scan.

Driver mapping sorts the changes you find by how important and how certain they are. A driver of change is a significant trend you can already observe that is expected to keep shaping the future. The toolkit places drivers on a grid along those two lines. Important, fairly certain drivers deserve attention in current planning. The timing of action depends on evidence, duties, risk and authority. Important but uncertain ones become the axes for scenarios: pick two, cross them, and describe the four worlds that result. A scenario is a plausible story, not a prediction. The toolkit suggests mixing hopeful and hard features in each world, then asking what three recommendations you would make if you lived there.

Intercultural concepts can help a team question its assumptions. In an illustration of Minimization, the team assumes a change will reach everyone the same way and plans for a typical person. In an illustration of Acceptance, the team notices that the same driver lands differently, for example that online services help some people and shut others out, and that its own sense of the likely future reflects its vantage point. In an illustration of Adaptation, the team changes how the work is done: plain-language sessions, interpreters, accessible materials, and self-advocates, families and partners helping shape the scenarios. These examples illustrate ideas from the Intercultural Development Continuum. A meeting practice or single statement does not establish a person’s or team’s assessed orientation.

Involving the people affected is part of the method. The Futures Toolkit says diverse perspectives make futures work stronger and that participants should include people affected now and in the future. It also cautions that public participation takes time, that bias in choosing participants must be avoided, and that people should hear why their time matters and how their input will be used. Tell willing participants what the exercise can change, how their input will be used and what will be recorded. Arrange access and communication support before the session. Check outreach, compensation and data handling with the responsible staff. A small workshop does not replace required public or Tribal consultation, and a few participants cannot speak for a whole community.
lessons.keyPoint: Scan widely, sort drivers by importance and certainty, and build scenarios from the uncertain ones. Invite the people a plan affects to imagine those futures with you, not only to review them afterward.
lessons.example: Practice case: Hannah, a program lead in the division, is organizing a half-day scenario session on the future of employment services for people with disabilities. The invitation list includes policy staff, two managers and a lead agency partner. Jun, a policy analyst on the team, points out that no self-advocates or family members are invited. The session is three weeks away, and the materials are dense slides. Authorized outreach and access support are available within the three weeks. Interested participants can choose whether to join, and no required formal engagement process is being replaced.
lessons.question: What should Hannah do before the session?
choices: Invite self-advocates and family members through groups they trust, rework the materials into plain language, and ask Jun whether he would like a role in shaping the agenda.
Keep this first session internal as planned, then send the draft scenarios to self-advocacy groups and family networks so they can comment on them.
Postpone the session for several months so the full program area can design a formal community engagement process with proper time and support.
feedback: This is the recommended step under the stated conditions. It invites willing participants to shape the scenarios while there is still time to change them. Confirm the support each person needs, and offer other ways to contribute. Jun can choose whether to take an additional role.
Comment on a draft is better than nothing, but the scenarios would already reflect staff assumptions. People affected would be reacting to futures others imagined for them.

Delay may be necessary when access, authority or required engagement cannot be arranged. In this case, support and authorized outreach are available for a smaller session. It can inform later work without claiming to represent everyone affected.
lessons.reflection: When you picture the future of your work, whose daily life do you picture? Whose experience would you need to ask about to see it more fully?
lessons.action: Write a scoping question for one area of your work with a time frame of at least five years. List three drivers of change you can already see and one group whose view of those drivers you have not yet heard.

check.question: In the scenario method described here, which drivers become the axes for the scenarios?
check.correct: Drivers that are very important to the question but uncertain.
wrong: Drivers that are very important and almost certain to happen.
Drivers the planning team agrees are most likely to occur.
check.feedback: Important and fairly certain drivers inform current planning. Important but uncertain drivers are where futures could split, so they make the best axes. Agreement on what is likely can hide the very uncertainty scenarios are meant to explore.

lessons.title: Testing today's decisions against different futures
objectives: Test a current decision against at least two scenarios and sort its parts as still working, no longer needed or needing change.
Identify which groups would be most exposed in each future and who has the fewest alternatives.
Name options that keep choices open, such as a second route, a pilot or a review date.
Separate the steps you control from the ones you can only influence.
lessons.teaching:
A decision made today has to work in futures you cannot choose. The Futures Toolkit calls its method policy stress-testing, also known as wind tunneling. You take a policy, strategy or project and imagine it operating in each of several scenarios. For each one, you ask whether the option still works there, whether it no longer serves a purpose, or whether it needs to change. The rule is to stay inside the logic of each scenario and not adjust the scenario to rescue a favored option. A simple version fits on one page: list your options down the side and two to four scenarios across the top, and in each box write still works, no longer needed or needs change. Add a last row for each scenario: who would be most exposed here, and what second route would they have?

An option that appears workable across the selected scenarios is a candidate for further consideration. Those scenarios do not cover every possible future, prove the option will succeed or authorize implementation. An option that works in only some scenarios may need changes or a contingency plan. Reconsider options that work in none. The toolkit notes that a single workshop is rough and ready, and that the facilitator's challenge is to avoid groupthink or defensiveness about favored options. Asking people who did not design an option to help test it can make the conversation easier.

Equity analysis includes asking who is most exposed in each future. These questions support, but do not replace, the analysis required by DHS policy. Exposure means who would be harmed first or most if conditions change, and who has the fewest alternatives. People who rely on one channel, one provider or one staff person are often more exposed than an average figure shows. So are people whose language, disability, income or location already makes access harder. For each scenario, ask who carries the burden, what evidence you have and whose experience is missing from it. Then ask people closest to the service, including front-line staff and partners, whether your picture matches theirs.

Options that keep choices open are often the most practical. A second service route, a pilot, a review date or a signal for reassessment can help a plan adjust. Each needs the right authority and resources. A phone route alone will not meet every access need. Before a trial, define access safeguards, monitoring and conditions for stopping it. Do not wait for a scheduled review when harm requires action. The toolkit's backcasting method adds a useful sort: mark each step as in your control, partly in your control or outside it, then plan how to influence the steps you do not control. Testing a decision does not change who makes it. Legal questions go to counsel. Work with responsible program, accessibility and procurement staff before changing services or making commitments to a vendor.
lessons.keyPoint: Test a decision against several futures, look hardest at who would be most exposed in each, and favor options that keep a second route, a review point or a clear way to change course.
lessons.example: Practice case: Abdi manages an economic assistance unit that plans to move all appointment scheduling online next year. The online system tested well with current users. Teresa, a county partner, mentions that a regional clinic where many people get in-person help may close, and that more older adults are applying for the first time. Abdi's team has one week to confirm the plan before an agreed project deadline. The team is authorized to keep the existing phone route during planning. Other required access arrangements remain in place, and the deadline does not authorize a service or contract change.
lessons.question: How should Abdi's team use the week?
choices: Confirm the online plan as designed, since user testing went well and the clinic closure and the rise in new applicants are still only possibilities.
Test the plan against a few futures with Teresa and front-line staff, keep a phone route open, and set a review date for how people reach appointments.
Ask the vendor to add guided help features to the online system so it can better serve first-time applicants and people without in-person help.
feedback: The testing was real, but it covered people already using the system. If the clinic closes, older and first-time applicants could lose their way in, and the plan has no fallback.

This is the recommended planning step. It tests assumptions and keeps an available route while the team checks access needs with affected people and responsible staff. The phone route and review date do not by themselves establish that the service is accessible or ready to change.

Guided features may help some users, but they do not address every reason people cannot use an online system. Assess other routes and required support too. Requests that would change a contract or commit resources need the appropriate authority.
lessons.reflection: Which decisions in your work depend on a single route, provider or person? What would it take to keep a second option open?
lessons.action: Choose one decision your team is about to make. Imagine it in two different futures and write down who would be most exposed in each. Propose one review point or second route, naming the approval and access support needed to put it in place.

check.question: During a stress-test, a favored option fails in one scenario. What does the method recommend?
check.correct: Keep the scenario as it is, then modify the option or hold it for the conditions where it works.
wrong: Adjust that scenario slightly so it better matches the conditions the option was designed for.
Set that scenario aside, since a plan only needs to work in the futures the team finds most likely.
check.feedback: Groups stay within each scenario's logic. An option that works in some futures but not others can be changed to hold up better or kept as a contingency plan. Bending the scenario hides the very risk the test was meant to find.

lessons.title: Stewardship: what a leader leaves in place
objectives: Identify commitments in your area whose effects will outlast your role and the futures they assume.
Plan how the scenarios, signals and review points behind a decision will stay with the team.
Build one equity routine into a standing agenda, template or review so it continues without you.
Describe what happened under your leadership, for whom, and what the team should keep, change or stop.
lessons.teaching:
Stewardship asks what will remain when you move on. Many decisions a senior leader makes outlast the leader: a multi-year agreement, a redesigned service, a new way of paying partners. Each one carries the futures its authors assumed, often without saying so. When those people leave, the next team inherits the commitment but not always the reasoning, and may keep defending a plan whose conditions have quietly changed. Stewardship means leaving the next team able to test a decision, not only carry it out.

Knowledge transfer is one part of stewardship, and another course covers it in depth. OPM’s succession planning guidance names shadowing, communities of practice and action learning among development methods. This lesson looks at something less often done: leaving the foresight behind a decision in place, so the people who come later can keep asking whether it still fits.

Leave the assumptions, signals and review dates with the decision. For each long-lived commitment, write down the future it assumes and the alternatives the team considered. Name the signals that would show conditions shifting, such as a change in the workforce, in who applies or in how people reach a service, and who would feel the shift first. Put review dates in a shared calendar, not in your memory, and say what each review should ask. Keep this reasoning with the appropriate official records and follow retention and access rules. Record necessary facts, not speculative judgments about people. Some official work requires individual information; use and share it only as authorized, rather than omitting it or assuming that removing names makes it public.

Shared routines can help practices continue after a leader leaves. A habit of asking who is missing, testing decisions against several futures or reviewing results with partners will fade if it depends on one person's reminder. Build one such question into a standing agenda, a decision template or a regular review with a responsible person, resources and a way to check whether it continues. Before you go, ask what happened under your leadership, for whom, and what the team should keep, change or stop. Stewardship includes continuity of functions and knowledge. Staffing decisions still follow applicable appointment, selection and labor requirements with responsible management and Human Resources. A handover does not promise a successor a position.
lessons.keyPoint: Long-lived decisions outlast the people who make them. Leave the assumed futures, the signals to watch and the review dates with each decision, and build equity routines into the team's standing work.
lessons.example: Practice case: Delphine, a deputy director in disability services, is leaving in four months. Two years ago her area signed a five-year agreement with lead agencies that assumes today's direct support workforce and current enrollment rates. Wendell, a manager, will carry the agreement forward and has asked what he most needs from her. Lead agency partners have started mentioning staff shortages. Delphine has time for one focused piece of work before she goes. She has already referred the shortage concerns to responsible program staff for timely review. The handover work will continue alongside any needed action.
lessons.question: What should Delphine leave in place for the agreement?
choices: Brief Wendell fully on the agreement's history, terms and partner contacts in a series of handover meetings across her last four months.
Write down the futures the agreement assumes, the signals of a shift and the review dates, then walk through them with Wendell and partners.
Push to renegotiate the agreement now to reflect the staff shortages, so Wendell does not inherit terms that may already be out of date.
feedback: Handover meetings are useful, especially when their reasoning is recorded and accessible to the next team. The proposed meetings emphasize history and terms; add the assumptions, signals and review responsibilities that help future staff reassess the agreement.

This is the recommended handover step. It preserves the reasoning and gives Wendell and authorized partners a way to reassess it. Identify who can act on each signal and use authorized channels for any nonpublic information.

Shortages may warrant prompt action or renegotiation through responsible staff. That review is already underway in this case. It does not remove the need to document assumptions and review responsibilities for the next team.
lessons.reflection: Which of your decisions will still be in effect after you move on? What would the next team need to know to question them well?
lessons.action: Choose one commitment in your area that will outlast your role. Write down the future it assumes, one alternative, the signal that would show a shift and who would feel it first, then propose a responsible reviewer and review date. Share only the information appropriate for that calendar, and flag conditions that require action sooner.

check.question: A long-lived decision is being handed to a new team. Which step best reflects stewardship as this lesson describes it?
check.correct: Leaving the assumed futures, signals to watch and review dates with the decision.
wrong: Leaving a full record of the decision's terms, history and partner contacts.
Leaving the decision firmly settled so the new team can carry it out quickly.
check.feedback: A record of terms and contacts helps, but it does not show what the decision depends on. Its assumptions, signals and review dates let the next team test it as conditions change, not just defend it.

cards.back: Preparing for several plausible futures instead of relying on one forecast, so plans can adjust as conditions change. It adds to formal strategic planning; it does not replace it.
Three views of the future: what we think will happen, what might happen instead and what we want to happen. Keeping all three in view keeps a plan honest.
A significant trend you can already observe that is expected to keep shaping the future, such as an aging population or changes in the workforce.
An early indicator of an issue that may become important later. Weak signals add to trend data and widen the range of futures a team considers.
The part of leadership concerned with what remains after you move on: the reasoning behind long-lived decisions, the signals and review dates to test them, and routines that continue without you.

aid.heading: Before you plan: frame the look ahead
items: Write a scoping question with a topic and a time frame of five years or more.
Name the future your current plan assumes and where that assumption came from.
List drivers of change you can already see, including social ones.
Plan authorized outreach to willing participants whose experience is missing, including access support and clear information about the use of their input.
Say plainly what the exercise can and cannot change.

aid.heading: Testing a decision against several futures
items: Sort drivers by how important and how certain they are, then cross the two most important uncertain ones to describe four plausible futures.
On one page, list options down the side and scenarios across the top, and mark each box still works, no longer needed or needs change.
Stay within each scenario's logic rather than bending it to save an option.
Add a last row: who would be most exposed in each future, and what second route would they have?
Propose a second route, pilot or review date with appropriate authority, access safeguards and conditions for earlier action.

aid.heading: What to leave in place
items: List the commitments that will outlast your role and the future each one assumes.
Name the signals that would show conditions shifting and who would feel it first.
Name the responsible reviewer, set review dates in an appropriate shared calendar and identify conditions that require action sooner.
Build a question such as who is missing into a standing agenda or template.
Ask what happened, for whom, and what the team should keep, change or stop.

sources.title: U.S. Government Accountability Office: Center for Strategic Foresight
sources.note: Supports that GAO keeps a Center for Strategic Foresight that analyzes trends affecting federal agencies, with trend papers looking five to 15 years ahead. Federal oversight context only.

sources.note: Supports the mention of communities of practice, shadowing and action learning as development methods in lesson 4. Federal guidance from 2005, used for concepts only; knowledge transfer is taught in depth elsewhere.

sources.note: Supports that Minnesota's leader competency guide lists strategic thinking and vision setting among skills for leaders of an organization. It sets expectations and does not teach foresight methods.
